data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Aggregation of independent non-experts suppresses idiosyncratic bias, but the checklist's explicitness introduces a systematic, correlated error: all panelists apply the same heuristic, so their errors are not independent. On tasks where the checklist's heuristic is wrong, the panel fails collectively and more reliably than the expert, whose intuition at least varies.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If panelists are trained to apply the checklist with judgment rather than mechanically, their errors may partially decorrelate.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the checklist is empirically validated and rarely wrong, the correlated-error subset is negligible.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert shares the same heuristic as the checklist (because both learned from the same domain), the expert's errors correlate too and the advantage vanishes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The panel's advantage depends on error independence: aggregation cancels noise. But a checklist is a shared procedure. If it encodes a wrong heuristic, every panelist follows it, producing correlated errors that aggregation amplifies rather than cancels. The single expert, relying on intuition, has no such forced correlation and may sometimes override the bad heuristic. Thus on the subset where the checklist is wrong, the panel is systematically less reliable than the expert\u2014not despite but because of the checklist's explicitness.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
